title: Atoms & X-Rays
subtitle: Zero-to-JEE-Advanced Visual Textbook: Rutherford Alpha Scattering, Distance of Closest Approach, Bohr Model of Hydrogen-Like Atoms, Spectral Series, Rydberg Formula, Atomic Recoil, Reduced Mass & X-Ray Spectra (Moseley's Law)
introduction:
💡 First-Time Reader Intuition: How Did We Map the Inside of an Invisible Atom?

At the start of the 20th century, J.J. Thomson proposed the “Plum Pudding Model”—imagining the atom as a soft sphere of positive charge with electrons embedded inside like seeds in a watermelon. In 1911, Ernest Rutherford, Hans Geiger, and Ernest Marsden fired high-speed alpha particles (${}_2^4\text{He}^{2+}$) at an ultra-thin gold foil. While $99.86\%$ passed straight through, about $1$ in $8000$ bounced almost straight backward ($\theta > 90^\circ$)!

Rutherford famously remarked: “It was almost as incredible as if you fired a 15-inch artillery shell at a piece of tissue paper and it came back and hit you!” This proved that $99.95\%$ of the atom's mass and all of its positive charge $+Ze$ are concentrated in a tiny central core called the Nucleus ($R \sim 10^{-15}\text{ m}$), while electrons orbit in vast empty space ($r \sim 10^{-10}\text{ m}$, $100,000\times$ larger!).

Why Classical Rutherford Orbits Were Doomed & How Niels Bohr Saved the Atom:
According to Maxwell's Electrodynamics, any accelerating charge (like an electron in circular orbit with $a_c = v^2/r$) must continuously radiate electromagnetic waves, lose energy, and spiral into the nucleus in $\sim 10^{-8}\text{ seconds}$! In 1913, Niels Bohr solved this by postulating quantized stationary orbits where angular momentum is an integer multiple of $\hbar = \frac{h}{2\pi}$!

topics.title: Rutherford Alpha-Particle Scattering, Distance of Closest Approach ($r_0$) & Impact Parameter ($b$)

prerequisites.label: Electrostatic Potential Energy U = k q₁ q₂ / r

topics.theoryHtml:
1.1 Distance of Closest Approach ($r_0$) in Head-On Collision
Energy Conservation in Head-On $\alpha$-Scattering ($\theta = 180^\circ$):
When an alpha particle (charge $q_\alpha = +2e$, initial kinetic energy $K_\alpha$) moves directly head-on toward a heavy stationary target nucleus of atomic number $Z$ (charge $Q = +Ze$), Coulomb repulsion slows it down until it momentarily stops ($v = 0$) at a minimum distance $r_0$ before rebounding by $180^\circ$.

At the turning point $r_0$, the entire initial kinetic energy $K_\alpha$ is converted into electrostatic potential energy:

$$K_\alpha = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{(2e)(Ze)}{r_0} \implies \boxed{r_0 = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{2 Z e^2}{K_\alpha} = \frac{2 k Z e^2}{\frac{1}{2}m_\alpha v_0^2}} \qquad \left(r_0 \propto \frac{Z}{K_\alpha}\right)$$
1.2 Impact Parameter ($b$) & Rutherford Scattering Formula
Definition (Impact Parameter $b$):
The perpendicular distance between the initial velocity vector of the $\alpha$-particle (far away from the nucleus) and the central line passing through the nucleus.
$$\boxed{b = \frac{Z e^2 \cot(\theta / 2)}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 K_\alpha} = \frac{r_0}{2}\cot\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)}$$
  • Head-on collision ($b = 0$): $\cot(\theta/2) = 0 \implies \frac{\theta}{2} = 90^\circ \implies \boxed{\theta = 180^\circ}$ (bounces straight back).
  • Large impact parameter ($b \to \infty$): $\theta \to 0^\circ$ (passes almost undeflected).
  • Rutherford Scattering Count at Angle $\theta$: The number of $\alpha$-particles scattered at angle $\theta$ is inversely proportional to the fourth power of $\sin(\theta/2)$:
    $$\boxed{N(\theta) \propto \frac{n t Z^2}{K_\alpha^2 \sin^4(\theta / 2)}}$$
topics.derivationHtml:
JEE Advanced Case: Distance of Closest Approach When the Target Nucleus (Mass M) Is Free to Recoil!

If the target nucleus of mass $M$ and charge $+Ze$ is NOT fixed, then at the instant of closest approach $r_{\min}$, both the projectile $(m, q_1, v_0)$ and the target $(M, q_2)$ move with the same common Center-of-Mass velocity $v_{\text{cm}} = \frac{mv_0}{m+M}$! Using Reduced Mass $\mu = \frac{m M}{m + M}$, only the kinetic energy in the COM frame ($K_{\text{rel}} = \frac{1}{2}\mu v_0^2 = \left(\frac{M}{m+M}\right)K_0$) converts into potential energy:

$$\frac{1}{2}\mu v_0^2 = \frac{k q_1 q_2}{r_{\min}} \implies \boxed{r_{\min} = \frac{2 k q_1 q_2}{\mu v_0^2} = \left(\frac{m + M}{M}\right)\frac{k q_1 q_2}{K_0}}$$

You must apply BOTH Conservation of Angular Momentum ($m v_0 b = m v_{\min} r_{\min}$) AND Conservation of Energy ($\frac{1}{2}mv_0^2 = \frac{1}{2}mv_{\min}^2 + \frac{k(2e)(Ze)}{r_{\min}}$) to solve for $r_{\min}$!

topics.title: Bohr's Model of Single-Electron Atoms (H, He+, Li2+): Postulates, Radius, Velocity, Time Period & Energy Levels
topics.theoryHtml:
2.1 Bohr's 3 Postulates & de Broglie Standing Wave Proof
  1. 1. Stationary Orbits & Centripetal Force: Electrons revolve around the nucleus ($+Ze$) in discrete circular orbits without radiating energy: $\boxed{\frac{m v^2}{r} = \frac{k Z e^2}{r^2}}$.
  2. 2. Quantization of Angular Momentum: Allowed orbits are those where orbital angular momentum $L$ is an integral multiple of $\hbar = \frac{h}{2\pi}$:
    $$\boxed{L = m v_n r_n = \frac{n h}{2\pi} = n\hbar} \qquad (n = 1, 2, 3, \dots = \text{Principal Quantum Number})$$
    de Broglie's Proof: For an electron wave not to cancel itself out by destructive interference, the circumference $2\pi r_n$ must contain an exact integer number of de Broglie wavelengths: $\boxed{2\pi r_n = n\lambda = n\left(\frac{h}{mv_n}\right) \iff m v_n r_n = \frac{nh}{2\pi}}$!
  3. 3. Frequency Condition for Photon Emission/Absorption: Jumping between $E_{n_2}$ and $E_{n_1}$ emits or absorbs a photon of energy $\boxed{\Delta E = E_{n_2} - E_{n_1} = h\nu = \frac{hc}{\lambda}}$.
2.2 Master Bohr Scaling Laws & Numerical Values (Valid for 1-Electron Species: $\text{H}, \text{He}^+, \text{Li}^{2+}, \text{Be}^{3+}$)
Physical QuantityExact FormulaScaling with $n$ & $Z$Ground State ($n=1, Z=1$) Value
1. Orbit Radius ($r_n$)$$r_n = \left(\frac{\varepsilon_0 h^2}{\pi m e^2}\right)\frac{n^2}{Z}$$$$\boxed{r_n \propto \frac{n^2}{Z}}$$$$\boxed{r_n = 0.529\,\frac{n^2}{Z}\text{ \AA}}$$
($a_0 = 0.529\text{ \AA}$ is Bohr Radius)
2. Orbital Speed ($v_n$)$$v_n = \left(\frac{e^2}{2\varepsilon_0 h}\right)\frac{Z}{n} = \left(\frac{c}{137}\right)\frac{Z}{n}$$$$\boxed{v_n \propto \frac{Z}{n}}$$$$\boxed{v_n = 2.18 \times 10^6\,\frac{Z}{n}\text{ m/s}}$$
3. Time Period ($T_n = \frac{2\pi r_n}{v_n}$)$T_n = 1.52 \times 10^{-16}\,\frac{n^3}{Z^2}\text{ s}$$$\boxed{T_n \propto \frac{n^3}{Z^2}}, \quad \boxed{f_n \propto \frac{Z^2}{n^3}}$$Current $I_n = ef_n \propto \frac{Z^2}{n^3}$
Mag. Moment $\mu_n = n\mu_B \propto n$
4. Kinetic, Potential & Total Energy$$\boxed{K_n = -E_n = -\frac{U_n}{2}}$$$$\boxed{E_n \propto -\frac{Z^2}{n^2}}$$$$\boxed{E_n = -13.6\,\frac{Z^2}{n^2}\text{ eV}}$$

Hydrogen Energy Levels ($Z = 1$) to Memorize by Heart:
• $n = 1$ (Ground State): $\mathbf{E_1 = -13.6\text{ eV}}$
• $n = 2$ ($1^{\text{st}}$ Excited State): $\mathbf{E_2 = -3.40\text{ eV}}$ ($\Delta E_{1\to 2} = 10.2\text{ eV}$)
• $n = 3$ ($2^{\text{nd}}$ Excited State): $\mathbf{E_3 = -1.51\text{ eV}}$ ($\Delta E_{1\to 3} = 12.09\text{ eV}, \; \Delta E_{2\to 3} = 1.89\text{ eV}$)
• $n = 4$ ($3^{\text{rd}}$ Excited State): $\mathbf{E_4 = -0.85\text{ eV}}$ ($\Delta E_{1\to 4} = 12.75\text{ eV}$)
topics.derivationHtml:
Step-by-Step Derivation of r_n, v_n, and the Golden Energy Ratio K_n : U_n : E_n = +1 : −2 : −1

1. Speed $v_n$ and Radius $r_n$: From $\frac{mv^2}{r} = \frac{kZe^2}{r^2} \implies m v^2 r = k Z e^2$. Divide this by Bohr's quantization $m v r = \frac{nh}{2\pi}$:

$$\frac{m v^2 r}{m v r} = v_n = \boxed{\frac{2\pi k Z e^2}{nh} \propto \frac{Z}{n}} \implies r_n = \frac{nh}{2\pi m v_n} = \boxed{\frac{n^2 h^2}{4\pi^2 m k Z e^2} \propto \frac{n^2}{Z}}$$

2. Energy Ratio ($K = -E = -U/2$): Since $\frac{mv^2}{r} = \frac{kZe^2}{r^2}$, kinetic energy is $K_n = \frac{1}{2}mv_n^2 = +\frac{kZe^2}{2r_n}$, while electrostatic potential energy (taking $U(\infty) = 0$) is $U_n = -\frac{kZe^2}{r_n} = -2K_n$. Adding them gives total energy:

$$\boxed{E_n = K_n + U_n = +\frac{kZe^2}{2r_n} - \frac{kZe^2}{r_n} = -\frac{kZe^2}{2r_n} = -K_n = \frac{U_n}{2}}$$

• Trap 1 (“$n^{\text{th}}$ Excited State” Means Orbit Number $n_{\text{orbit}} = n + 1$!):
    • Ground State: $n = 1$
    • $1^{\text{st}}$ Excited State: $n = 2$ (NOT $n = 1$!)
    • $2^{\text{nd}}$ Excited State: $n = 3$
    • $k^{\text{th}}$ Excited State: $n = k + 1$!
  • Trap 2 (What Happens If Potential Energy at Infinity Is Shifted From $U(\infty) = 0$ to $U(\infty) = +E_0$?): Shifting the zero reference of potential energy adds $+E_0$ to $U_n$ and $+E_0$ to Total Energy $E_n$, but Kinetic Energy $K_n = \frac{1}{2}mv_n^2$ and Energy Differences $\Delta E = E_{n_2} - E_{n_1}$ remain 100% UNCHANGED!

topics.title: Hydrogen Spectral Series (Lyman to Pfund), Rydberg Formula, Number of Spectral Lines, Atomic Recoil & Reduced Mass
topics.theoryHtml:
3.1 Rydberg Formula & The 5 Spectral Series of Hydrogen
$$\textbf{Rydberg Wave-Number Formula } \left(\bar{\nu} = \frac{1}{\lambda}\right): \qquad \boxed{\frac{1}{\lambda} = R Z^2 \left(\frac{1}{n_1^2} - \frac{1}{n_2^2}\right)} \qquad (n_2 > n_1)$$

Where Rydberg constant $R = \frac{m e^4}{8\varepsilon_0^2 h^3 c} = 1.097 \times 10^7\text{ m}^{-1}$, and the Golden Reciprocal to Memorize is $\boxed{\frac{1}{R} \approx 911.6\text{ \AA} \approx 912\text{ \AA}}$!

Spectral SeriesLower Level ($n_1$)Upper Levels ($n_2$)EM Spectrum RegionFirst Line ($\lambda_{\max}, n_1+1 \to n_1$)Series Limit ($\lambda_{\min}, \infty \to n_1$)
1. Lyman Series$$n_1 = 1$$$2, 3, 4, \dots, \infty$Ultraviolet (UV)$\frac{4}{3R} = 1216\text{ \AA}$ ($L_\alpha$)$\frac{1}{R} = 912\text{ \AA}$
2. Balmer Series$$n_1 = 2$$$3, 4, 5, \dots, \infty$Visible Light$\frac{36}{5R} = 6563\text{ \AA}$ ($H_\alpha$)$\frac{4}{R} = 3646\text{ \AA}$
3. Paschen Series$$n_1 = 3$$$4, 5, 6, \dots, \infty$Near Infrared (IR)$\frac{144}{7R}$$\frac{9}{R} = 8204\text{ \AA}$
4. Brackett Series$$n_1 = 4$$$5, 6, 7, \dots, \infty$Mid Infrared (IR)$\frac{400}{9R}$$\frac{16}{R}$
5. Pfund Series$$n_1 = 5$$$6, 7, 8, \dots, \infty$Far Infrared (IR)$\frac{900}{11R}$$\frac{25}{R}$
3.2 Number of Spectral Lines, Atomic Recoil Speed & Reduced Mass Correction
  • 1. Maximum Number of Spectral Lines From Sample of Many Atoms:
    • From level $n$ down to ground state ($n_1 = 1$): $\boxed{N_{\text{lines}} = \binom{n}{2} = \frac{n(n - 1)}{2}}$.
    • From upper level $n_2$ down to lower level $n_1$: $\boxed{N_{\text{lines}} = \frac{(n_2 - n_1)(n_2 - n_1 + 1)}{2}}$.
    • From a SINGLE isolated atom in level $n$: Maximum possible photons emitted in one cascade is $\boxed{N_{\text{single atom}} = n - 1}$!
  • 2. Recoil Speed & Recoil Kinetic Energy of Atom During Photon Emission:
    When a stationary atom of mass $M$ undergoes transition $\Delta E$, momentum conservation ($0 = p_{\text{atom}} - p_{\text{photon}}$) requires $M v_{\text{recoil}} = \frac{h}{\lambda} = \frac{\Delta E}{c}$:
    $$\boxed{v_{\text{recoil}} = \frac{h}{M\lambda} = \frac{\Delta E}{M c}} \qquad \text{and} \qquad \boxed{K_{\text{recoil}} = \frac{p^2}{2M} = \frac{(\Delta E)^2}{2 M c^2}}$$
  • 3. Finite Nuclear Mass ($M$) & Reduced Mass ($\mu = \frac{m_e M}{m_e + M}$):
    If the nucleus of mass $M$ is not infinitely heavy (e.g., Positronium $e^- e^+$ where $M = m_e \implies \mu = \frac{m_e}{2}$, or Deuterium ${}_1^2\text{H}$), replace electron mass $m_e$ with $\mu$: $$\boxed{r_n' = \left(\frac{m_e}{\mu}\right)r_n, \qquad E_n' = \left(\frac{\mu}{m_e}\right)E_n, \qquad R' = \left(\frac{\mu}{m_e}\right)R}$$For Positronium ($\mu = m_e / 2$): Ground state energy is $-\frac{13.6}{2} = \mathbf{-6.8\text{ eV}}$ and radius is $2 \times 0.529 = \mathbf{1.058\text{ \AA}}$!
topics.derivationHtml:
Combination Formula for Successive Transitions: 1 / λ₁₃ = 1 / λ₁₂ + 1 / λ₂₃

Since energy differences add ($\Delta E_{3\to 1} = \Delta E_{3\to 2} + \Delta E_{2\to 1}$) and $\Delta E = \frac{hc}{\lambda}$, dividing by $hc$ gives Ritz's Combination Principle for wavelengths:

$$\boxed{\frac{1}{\lambda_{3\to 1}} = \frac{1}{\lambda_{3\to 2}} + \frac{1}{\lambda_{2\to 1}} \implies \lambda_{3\to 1} = \frac{\lambda_{3\to 2}\,\lambda_{2\to 1}}{\lambda_{3\to 2} + \lambda_{2\to 1}}}$$

topics.jeeTraps: • Trap (Inelastic Collision of a Neutron/Electron with a Stationary Hydrogen Atom!): Suppose a neutron of kinetic energy $K$ collides head-on with a stationary Hydrogen atom (equal mass $m$) in its ground state ($-13.6\text{ eV}$). Can a neutron with $K = 10.2\text{ eV}$ excite the H-atom to $n = 2$? NO! By momentum conservation, the maximum kinetic energy lost in a head-on completely inelastic collision between two equal masses is only HALF of the initial kinetic energy ($\Delta K_{\max} = \frac{1}{2}K$)! Thus to supply $\Delta E = 10.2\text{ eV}$ to the H-atom, the incident neutron (or H-atom) must have at least $\boxed{K_{\min} = 2 \times 10.2\text{ eV} = 20.4\text{ eV}}$!

topics.title: X-Rays: Coolidge Tube Production, Continuous Cut-Off Wavelength (λ_min), Characteristic X-Rays & Moseley's Law
topics.theoryHtml:
4.1 Coolidge Tube & Continuous (Bremsstrahlung) X-Ray Spectrum
How Continuous X-Rays Are Produced & Cut-Off Wavelength ($\lambda_{\min}$):
Electrons emitted by a heated filament are accelerated through a high voltage $V$ ($10 ext{ kV}$ to $100 ext{ kV}$), acquiring kinetic energy $K = eV$, and slam into a heavy metal target (Tungsten or Molybdenum). When an electron is suddenly decelerated by the Coulomb field of a target nucleus, it radiates Bremsstrahlung (“braking radiation”) X-rays. If an electron loses $100\%$ of its kinetic energy $eV$ in a single collision, it emits a photon of maximum frequency $ u_{\max}$ and minimum (cut-off) wavelength $\lambda_{\min}$:
$$e V = h u_{\max} = rac{h c}{\lambda_{\min}} \implies oxed{\lambda_{\min} = rac{h c}{e V} = rac{12400}{V ext{ (in Volts)}} ext{ \AA}}$$

Crucial Rule: The cut-off wavelength $\lambda_{\min}$ depends ONLY on the accelerating voltage $V$—it is 100% independent of the target metal's atomic number $Z$! (Whereas X-ray intensity is controlled independently by the filament heating current).

4.2 Characteristic X-Rays ($K_\alpha, K_ eta, L_\alpha$) & Moseley's Law
How Characteristic X-Ray Spikes Are Produced:
When a high-speed incident electron knocks out an inner-shell electron (say from the $K$-shell, $n = 1$) of the target atom, an electron from a higher shell ($L$-shell $n=2 o K_\alpha$ line, or $M$-shell $n=3 o K_ eta$ line) drops into the vacancy, emitting a sharp X-ray line whose wavelength is a unique fingerprint of the target element $Z$!
$$ extbf{Moseley's Law (1913):} \qquad oxed{\sqrt{ u} = a(Z - b)} \qquad ext{where } oxed{ u = R c (Z - b)^2 \left( rac{1}{n_1^2} - rac{1}{n_2^2} ight)}$$
  • For the $K_\alpha$ Line ($n_2 = 2 o n_1 = 1$): Only $1$ electron remains in the $K$-shell to screen the nucleus $+Ze$, so the screening constant is $ oxed{b = 1}$:
    $$ oxed{ rac{1}{\lambda_{K_\alpha}} = rac{3}{4} R (Z - 1)^2 \implies u_{K_\alpha} = rac{3}{4} R c (Z - 1)^2}$$
  • Bragg's Law for X-Ray Crystal Diffraction: When X-rays strike crystal planes separated by interplanar spacing $d$ at glancing angle $ heta$ (measured from the crystal surface, NOT the normal!): $ oxed{2 d \sin heta = n\lambda}$.
topics.derivationHtml:
Why the K_β Line Has Higher Energy (Shorter Wavelength) Than K_α, and Combination Rule ν_Kβ = ν_Kα + ν_Lα

Since $K_\alpha$ is the jump $n=2 o n=1$, $K_ eta$ is $n=3 o n=1$, and $L_\alpha$ is $n=3 o n=2$, energy conservation ($E_3 - E_1 = (E_3 - E_2) + (E_2 - E_1)$) immediately gives:

$$ oxed{ u_{K_ eta} = u_{K_\alpha} + u_{L_\alpha} \iff rac{1}{\lambda_{K_ eta}} = rac{1}{\lambda_{K_\alpha}} + rac{1}{\lambda_{L_\alpha}}}$$

Because $\Delta E_{3 o 1} > \Delta E_{2 o 1}$, the $K_ eta$ photon ALWAYS has higher frequency and shorter wavelength ($\lambda_{K_ eta} < \lambda_{K_\alpha}$) than the $K_\alpha$ photon!

topics.jeeTraps: • Trap (Look at the Left-to-Right Order of $K_\beta$ and $K_\alpha$ Spikes on an Intensity vs. $\lambda$ Graph!): Since wavelength $\lambda$ increases from left to right and $\lambda_{K_\beta} < \lambda_{K_\alpha}$, the LEFT spike (shorter $\lambda$) is ALWAYS $K_\beta$, and the RIGHT taller spike (longer $\lambda$) is ALWAYS $K_\alpha$! Furthermore, if you increase the tube voltage $V$, $\lambda_{\min}$ shifts to the left, while the positions of the $K_\alpha$ and $K_\beta$ peaks do NOT shift at all!

summary:
• Rutherford Scattering: $r_0 = \frac{2kZe^2}{K_\alpha}$, $b = \frac{r_0}{2}\cot(\theta/2)$, $N(\theta) \propto \frac{1}{\sin^4(\theta/2)}$.
  • Bohr Model: $L = \frac{nh}{2\pi}$ ($2\pi r_n = n\lambda$); $r_n = 0.529\frac{n^2}{Z}\text{ \AA}$; $v_n = 2.18 \times 10^6\frac{Z}{n}\text{ m/s}$; $E_n = -13.6\frac{Z^2}{n^2}\text{ eV}$ ($K = -E = -U/2$).
  • Spectra: $\frac{1}{\lambda} = RZ^2\left(\frac{1}{n_1^2} - \frac{1}{n_2^2}\right)$ ($1/R \approx 912\text{ \AA}$); Spectral lines $= \frac{n(n-1)}{2}$; Recoil speed $v = \frac{h}{M\lambda}$.
  • X-Rays: Cut-off $\lambda_{\min} = \frac{12400}{V}\text{ \AA}$; Moseley's Law $\sqrt{\nu} = a(Z - b)$ with $b = 1$ for $K_\alpha$.

questions.prompt: In a hydrogen atom, what is the ratio of the radius of the $3^{\text{rd}}$ Bohr orbit ($n = 3$) to the radius of the $1^{\text{st}}$ Bohr orbit ($n = 1$), and what is the ratio of electron speeds ($v_3 : v_1$) in these two orbits?
questions.explanation: Since $r_n \propto n^2$, we have $r_3 : r_1 = 3^2 : 1^2 = 9 : 1$. Since $v_n \propto \frac{1}{n}$, we have $v_3 : v_1 = \frac{1}{3} : 1 = 1 : 3$.

questions.prompt: A sample of hydrogen gas has its atoms excited to the $3^{\text{rd}}$ excited state ($n = 4$). What is the maximum number of distinct spectral lines that can be emitted as the atoms de-excite to the ground state?
questions.explanation: Remember: the $3^{\text{rd}}$ excited state corresponds to principal quantum number $n = 3 + 1 = 4$! Thus the total number of distinct spectral lines is $N = \frac{n(n-1)}{2} = \frac{4(4-1)}{2} = 6$.

questions.prompt: What is the ratio of the shortest wavelength of the Balmer series ($\lambda_{\min, \text{Balmer}}$) to the shortest wavelength of the Lyman series ($\lambda_{\min, \text{Lyman}}$) in the hydrogen spectrum?
questions.explanation: Shortest wavelength (series limit) occurs for $n_2 = \infty \to n_1$, where $\frac{1}{\lambda_{\min}} = \frac{R}{n_1^2} \implies \lambda_{\min} = \frac{n_1^2}{R} \propto n_1^2$. For Balmer ($n_1 = 2$) and Lyman ($n_1 = 1$), the ratio is $2^2 : 1^2 = 4 : 1$.

questions.prompt: An X-ray Coolidge tube operates at an accelerating potential difference of $V = 24.8\text{ kV}$. What is the minimum (cut-off) wavelength $\lambda_{\min}$ of the continuous X-rays produced by the tube? (Use $hc = 12400\text{ eV}\cdot\text{\AA}$)

If the wavelength of the $K_\alpha$ characteristic X-ray line emitted by an element of atomic number $Z = 41$ is $\lambda$, then what is the atomic number $Z'$ of another element that emits a $K_\alpha$ line of wavelength $4\lambda$?
questions.explanation: By Moseley's Law for the $K_\alpha$ line ($b = 1$), $\frac{1}{\lambda} \propto (Z - 1)^2$. Thus $\frac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_1} = \frac{4\lambda}{\lambda} = 4 = \left(\frac{Z_1 - 1}{Z_2 - 1}\right)^2 \implies \frac{41 - 1}{Z_2 - 1} = 2 \implies Z_2 - 1 = 20 \implies Z_2 = 21$.

questions.prompt: A stationary Hydrogen atom (mass $M$) in its first excited state ($n = 2$) emits a photon and drops to the ground state ($n = 1$). In terms of the Rydberg constant $R$, Planck's constant $h$, and mass $M$, what is the recoil speed $v$ acquired by the Hydrogen atom?
questions.explanation: For $n=2 \to n=1$ in Hydrogen ($Z=1$), $\frac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(1 - \frac{1}{4}\right) = \frac{3R}{4}$. By conservation of linear momentum, $p_{\text{atom}} = p_{\text{photon}} \implies M v = \frac{h}{\lambda} = \frac{3Rh}{4} \implies v = \frac{3Rh}{4M}$.
